title: The Bronze at Campo de' Fiori: a Sculptor of the Lay Republic
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Rome, birth in a carbonaro's house
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In a Rome still governed by the Pope a son is born to Filippo Ferrari, sculptor and engraver, who carried a carbonaro's oath and fought for the Roman Republic, and to Maria Luisa Pasini. The boy is handed the trade in the same room where he is handed the politics: chisels, plaster, the memory of 1849 and of foreign guns restoring a pontiff over a republic five months old. He will spend eighty-four years in this city, and he will put its quarrel with the Church into bronze in the middle of a market square.
suggested_refs: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Ferrari, Ettore', on Filippo Ferrari, scultore e incisore, 1814-1897
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Ferrari, Ettore'

stops.name: Rome, the insurrection against the papal government
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by Treccani; his role in the rising is not specified in any source consulted
stops.campa: At twenty-two he takes part in the rising the republican committees raise inside the walls against the papal government. It fails, and no source records what he did in it. The temporal power stands, the conspirators scatter, and the young sculptor goes back to the clay carrying a defeat that does not leave him. What the barricade could not do to the papacy he will do later in bronze, on public ground, at municipal expense, with the city assembled to watch the sheet come off.
suggested_refs: The October 1867 republican insurrection in papal Rome
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Ferrari, Ettore'

stops.name: Rome, the Accademia di San Luca: the Albacini prize
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Treccani; month and day unrecorded, defaulted to January
stops.campa: He enters the Albacini competition of the Accademia di San Luca with a terracotta sketch and wins it, and with it a scholarship of two years. The Accademia is the papal city's own school of art, and the boy who was in the streets against the papacy the autumn before now draws its stipend. He takes the training whole: anatomy, modelling, the historical subject handled with the gravity the century demands. It is the last apprenticeship served in Rome before Rome becomes Italian.
suggested_refs: The Albacini competition of the Accademia Nazionale di San Luca; the terracotta 'Labano accoglie amorevolmente Giacobbe'
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Ferrari, Ettore'

stops.name: Rome, the diploma and the romantic figures
stops.date_confidence: year attested by it.wikipedia; month and day unrecorded, defaulted to January
stops.campa: He graduates with the historical-romantic manner already personal to him: Ildegonda and Bruto in 1870, Stefano Porcari, Ermengarda in 1874, figures drawn from Manzoni and from the Roman republican past and modelled with a literary, nervous pathos. Rome by now is the capital of the Kingdom and the Pope is shut inside the Vatican, and every piazza in Italy is an argument waiting for a statue to settle it. Ferrari has the manner and the politics. The commissions have not yet come.
suggested_refs: Ildegonda and Bruto (1870), Stefano Porcari, Ermengarda (1874)
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Ferrari, Ettore'

segments.name: Councillor, and the Commissions from Abroad

stops.name: Rome, the Campidoglio: elected by the democrats
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Treccani; month and day of the election unrecorded, defaulted to January
stops.campa: The democrats send him to the city council of Rome, and he will sit there, with interruptions, for thirty years, in the same season that his Iacopo Ortis takes an honourable mention at the National Exhibition in Naples. From here the two careers run in one body: the sculptor who supplies the new state with its public memory, and the councillor who votes on where that memory is permitted to stand. He is thirty-two, and he will still be sitting on this council thirty years from now.
suggested_refs: The Rome city council rolls, 1877-1907; Iacopo Ortis at the Naples National Exhibition
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Ferrari, Ettore'

stops.name: Bucharest, before the University: Ion Heliade Radulescu
stops.date_confidence: Treccani dates the work 1877; it.wikipedia gives no year; month unrecorded, defaulted to January. No source places Ferrari in Bucharest.
stops.campa: Romania, a young Latin kingdom shopping in Italy for its ancestry, commissions from him a monument to Ion Heliade Radulescu, poet and founder of its modern letters; the statue is set before the University building in the centre of Bucharest. It is the first of his works to leave Italy, and it fixes the pattern of everything foreign that follows: nations assembling a secular pantheon send to Rome for a republican sculptor. The Romanians will come back to him twice, for Ovid at Tomis and for Trajan at Cluj.
suggested_refs: The Heliade Radulescu monument in Piata Universitatii, Bucharest
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Ferrari, Ettore'

stops.name: Rome, Campo de' Fiori: the first Bruno refused
stops.date_confidence: year attested by it.wikipedia; month and day unrecorded, defaulted to January
stops.campa: A committee wants Giordano Bruno standing on the square where the Inquisition burned him in 1600, and Ferrari draws it. The first design is refused as too polemical toward the Catholic Church, too plainly an accusation cut for the Vatican to read across the river. The refusal tells him the ground is the right ground. He will work at this square for ten years, through committees and subscriptions and governments, until a version passes that is no less an accusation, only better armoured.
suggested_refs: The rejected first design for the Giordano Bruno monument, 1879

stops.name: Turin, Cum Spartaco pugnavit takes the first prize
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Treccani; month unrecorded, defaulted to January. The Venice competition it mentions was announced September 1879.
stops.campa: Cum Spartaco pugnavit takes first prize at the National Exhibition in Turin: the slave who fought beside Spartacus, the title lifted from the Roman formula for a disgrace and given the bearing of a hero. In the same season he wins the competition for the equestrian monument to Vittorio Emanuele II at Venice, forty-eight designs entered against his. The republican who models rebel slaves will model the king as well, and take the fee for both without explaining himself.
suggested_refs: Cum Spartaco pugnavit, plaster, first prize at the Turin National Exhibition 1880
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Ferrari, Ettore'

stops.name: Rome, the lodge Rienzi: the initiation
stops.date_confidence: attested to the summer of 1881; day unrecorded, defaulted to 1 July. The meeting place of the lodge in 1881 is unknown: the Grande Oriente did not occupy Palazzo Giustiniani until 1901, so a generic Rome pin is used.
stops.campa: Proposed by Ulisse Bacci, he is initiated into the lodge Rienzi of the Grande Oriente d'Italia. He has been married a year, to Maria Carolina Frey von Freienstein, and his first son Gian Giacomo is born the same year; a second son will be christened Giordano Bruno. The lodge puts his anticlericalism inside an institution, with a discipline to keep and a correspondence reaching every capital in Europe. From this room, over the next forty-eight years, he will rise to the head of Italian Freemasonry and stay there.
suggested_refs: The lodge Rienzi of the Grande Oriente d'Italia, Rome
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Ferrari, Ettore'

segments.name: The Chamber and the King on Horseback

stops.name: Rome, the second prize for the king's monument
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Perodi's chronicle; month unrecorded, defaulted to January
stops.campa: Rome opens the competition for its own monument to Vittorio Emanuele II, the vast altar the capital means to raise to the first king of Italy, and Ferrari enters it with the architect Pio Piacentini. They take the second prize, thirty thousand lire. The first goes to another hand. He has the Venetian king already and will never have the Roman one, and the commission that gets away from him here is the one that would have made him the official sculptor of the state.
stops.quote: il secondo di lire 30,000 a quello degli artisti Ettore Ferrari e Pio Piacentini
stops.quote_source: Emma Perodi, Roma italiana 1870-1895 (Bontempelli, Rome, 1896), chapter 'Il 1882'
suggested_refs: The 1882 competition for the Rome monument to Vittorio Emanuele II

stops.name: Spoleto, deputy for the college of Perugia II
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The college of Perugia II returns him to the Chamber of Deputies with three thousand and three preferences, and he takes a seat on the extreme left: against colonial expansion, against the Triple Alliance, against Crispi. He is reconfirmed in 1886 and again in 1890 and sits through three legislatures. The sculptor of public monuments is now a voice in the assembly that pays for them, and he works both instruments toward one programme, an Italy that owes the Church nothing at all.
suggested_refs: The parliamentary record of the XV, XVI and XVII legislatures
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Ferrari, Ettore'

stops.name: Venice, the Riva degli Schiavoni: the king on horseback
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1 May 1887 by it.wikipedia; Ferrari's own presence at the ceremony is not stated in any source consulted
stops.campa: On the Riva degli Schiavoni, between the lagoon and the Doge's city, his bronze Vittorio Emanuele II is unveiled before Umberto I and Queen Margherita, cast in Rome by Alessandro Nelli. Venice has been Italian for twenty-one years and takes its king in the coin of the Renaissance, mounted, at the water's edge, with the crowd of a dead maritime republic at the horse's feet. The republican deputy stands in the ceremonial company of the monarchy whose crown he will shortly put under Garibaldi's boot.
stops.quote: Nella prima città s'inaugurava il monumento a Vittorio Emanuele, modellato da Ettore Ferrari e fuso qui dal Nelli;
suggested_refs: The equestrian Vittorio Emanuele II on the Riva degli Schiavoni, Venice, cast by Alessandro Nelli

stops.name: Constanta, Piata Ovidiu: the exile in bronze
stops.date_confidence: modelled 1879 per Treccani, unveiled August 1887 per ro.wikipedia; day of the unveiling unrecorded, defaulted to the first
stops.campa: The Ovid he modelled in 1879 is unveiled in bronze in the square before the town hall of Constanta, the Tomis to which Augustus banished the poet and where he died without seeing Rome again. The prefect Remus Opreanu receives it for Romania. A Latin kingdom on the Black Sea takes formal possession of the most famous deportee in its soil, and the man who made him is an exile of another kind, a republican serving a monarchy. This is the work of his that will be copied and sent home to Abruzzo.
suggested_refs: The Ovid statue in Piata Ovidiu, Constanta, facing the former City Hall
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Ferrari, Ettore'

stops.name: Rome, Campo de' Fiori: the bronze raised on the burning place
stops.date_confidence: 9 June 1889 per it.wikipedia and the 1911 Britannica; Emma Perodi's 1896 chronicle gives 9 July 1889. Contradiction left open.
stops.campa: The bronze goes up on the spot where Giordano Bruno was burned on 17 February 1600, hooded, turned to face the Vatican across the river. Delegations of students, freethinkers, radicals and anticlerical societies from Italy and abroad fill the square; the subscription that paid for the casting was driven by students of the University of Rome. Leo XIII spends the day of the unveiling fasting and praying against it. For the rest of Ferrari's life this square is his one universally known work.
stops.quote: Il dì 8 luglio giunsero a Roma le rappresentanze delle università italiane ed estere, dei comuni e delle società che avevano aderito all'invito del Comitato per il monumento a Giordano Bruno, e il 9 era solennemente inaugurato questo monumento scolpito da Ettore Ferrari che aveva dato tanto da fare e da dire.
stops.quote_source: Emma Perodi, Roma italiana 1870-1895, chapter 'Il 1889' (this chronicle dates the unveiling 9 July; other sources give 9 June)
suggested_refs: The Giordano Bruno monument, Campo de' Fiori, Rome, unveiled 1889

stops.name: Rome, Campo de' Fiori: the eight medallions
stops.date_confidence: the medallions are part of the monument unveiled in 1889; the concealed Luther was identified only in 1991
stops.campa: Around the pedestal he sets eight medallion portraits of the Church's other defendants: Paolo Sarpi, Tommaso Campanella, Petrus Ramus, Lucilio Vanini, Aonio Paleario, Miguel Servet, John Wycliffe, Jan Hus. Campanella was broken by the same Roman Inquisition that burned the man standing above them; Vanini was strangled and burned at Toulouse. Worked into the Vanini relief, and unnoticed for a hundred years, Ferrari hides a small portrait of Martin Luther, set on the papacy's doorstep and never declared.
suggested_refs: The eight dissident medallions of the Bruno pedestal; the concealed Luther in the Vanini relief

stops.name: Rome, the Pact of Rome
stops.date_confidence: attested to May 1890 by Treccani; day unrecorded, defaulted to the first
stops.campa: He organises in Rome a congress of the whole opposition, and it closes with the Pact of Rome, signed by radicals, socialists, irredentists and republicans: one front against the government, assembled by the man who has just put Bruno over the flower market. On the thirtieth of June he speaks in the Chamber on article eleven of the bill for the municipal government of Rome, and the following first of May he walks with the workers at Santa Croce in Gerusalemme and answers for it to the deputies.
suggested_refs: The Pact of Rome, May 1890
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Ferrari, Ettore'

stops.name: Vatican, the encyclical Ab Apostolici
stops.date_confidence: attested to October 1890; day unrecorded, defaulted to the first
stops.campa: From the other bank of the river Leo XIII answers the statue in an encyclical. Ab Apostolici condemns the monument as eminently sectarian and charges it with aiming to insult the papacy under cover of honouring a philosopher. A pope has condemned a piece of municipal statuary by name, from the Apostolic Palace, in a document addressed to the bishops of the world. Neither party proposes to move. The statue keeps its back to the market and its face to the Vatican.
suggested_refs: Leo XIII, encyclical Ab Apostolici, October 1890

stops.name: Rome, Maestro Venerabile of the lodge Rienzi
stops.date_confidence: year attested by it.wikipedia; month unrecorded, defaulted to January. Meeting place of the lodge in 1892 unknown, generic Rome pin used.
stops.campa: He is raised to Maestro Venerabile of the lodge Rienzi, the chair from which the Grande Oriente d'Italia customarily draws its officers, and the sculptor becomes an officer of the Order. In the same year the bronze Garibaldi is cast for Pisa. The two lives run on one timetable now: clay in the morning, the Chamber or the Campidoglio by day, the lodge at night. The country that would not obey Garibaldi while he lived keeps ordering him by the ton in bronze.
suggested_refs: The Venerable Mastership of the lodge Rienzi, 1892

stops.name: Pisa, Piazza Garibaldi: the series begins
stops.date_confidence: year attested by it.wikipedia; month and day unrecorded, defaulted to January
stops.campa: The bronze Garibaldi is unveiled in the square that carries his name, on the Arno. Ferrari has begun the series that defines his middle years: Garibaldi in marble at Vicenza, in bronze here, at Cortona and Tortona and Macerata, at Massa Marittima, at Bevagna, at Rovigo on horseback. He knows exactly what he is manufacturing. The general is the one figure of the Risorgimento that the monarchy and the republicans can both claim, and every town wants him in its piazza with a sword.
suggested_refs: The Garibaldi of Piazza Garibaldi, Pisa, 1892
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Ferrari, Ettore'

stops.name: Rome, Quintino Sella before the Ministry of Finance
stops.date_confidence: attested to 2 March 1893 by Perodi's chronicle
stops.campa: His Quintino Sella is inaugurated in front of the Ministry of Finance, the man of the right who balanced the kingdom's books set down at the door of the department he ran. Ferrari, of the far left, models him without irony; the new state's memory is a public commission and he takes it as one. The deputy who votes against the government's budgets supplies the government's dead with their bronze, and no committee in Italy has yet found a reason to look elsewhere for a sculptor.
stops.quote: Il monumento era stato modellato da Ettore Ferrari e fuso in bronzo.
stops.quote_source: Emma Perodi, Roma italiana 1870-1895, chapter 'Il 1893', on the Quintino Sella monument
suggested_refs: The Quintino Sella monument before the Ministry of Finance, Rome, inaugurated 2 March 1893
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Ferrari, Ettore'

stops.name: Macerata, the Garibaldi of the provinces
stops.date_confidence: year attested by it.wikipedia and Treccani; month unrecorded, defaulted to January. Cortona and Tortona rest on Treccani alone.
stops.campa: The Garibaldi of Macerata is inaugurated, one of three that the year sends out of his studio, with Cortona and Tortona taking theirs in the same season. The provincial commissions arrive now in numbers: committees of veterans, municipal councils, subscription lists printed in local papers, each town wanting the general at the head of its own square. Ferrari supplies them from Rome, varying the attitude and holding the reading constant, the volunteer of the Thousand and not the king's soldier.
suggested_refs: The Garibaldi monuments of Macerata, Cortona and Tortona, 1895
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Ferrari, Ettore'

stops.name: Rovigo, the stirrups shaped as a crown
stops.date_confidence: attested to 15 November 1896 by it.wikipedia's article on the monument; Treccani's 1897 is an error
stops.campa: The equestrian Garibaldi is unveiled at Rovigo on the fifteenth of November, and the town has it because Rome would not. Ferrari cast the stirrups on which the general's boots rest in the shape of the crown of the House of Savoy, so that the volunteer rides with the monarchy underfoot. The intended site was the capital. The statue was sent instead to the Polesine, exiled for an insolence in bronze that no committee could unsay without melting down the horse and beginning again.
suggested_refs: The equestrian Garibaldi of Rovigo, inaugurated 15 November 1896

stops.name: Rome, the chair of sculpture and the Grand Secretariat
stops.date_confidence: the chair is attested to 1896 by Treccani; the Grand Secretariat is dated 1896 by it.wikipedia and 1897 by en.wikipedia, which also names Adriano Lemmi, whose tenure had ended on 1 June 1896. Address of the Regio Istituto not established: generic Rome pin.
stops.campa: He is given the chair of sculpture at the Regio Istituto di belle arti in Rome, and in the same period the Grande Oriente d'Italia makes him its Grand Secretary under Ernesto Nathan. The state he opposes in the Chamber employs him to teach its sculptors; the Order the state distrusts employs him to keep its books. His Terenzio Mamiani goes to Pesaro this year. At fifty-one he holds a chair, a secretariat, a council seat and a studio, and gives up none of them.
suggested_refs: The chair of sculpture at the Regio Istituto di belle arti, Rome, 1896; the Mamiani monument at Pesaro
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Ferrari, Ettore'

stops.name: Vicosoprano, the monument to Engel
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Treccani; month unrecorded, defaulted to January. Coordinate is an approximate village pin for Vicosoprano; the exact site is not given.
stops.campa: A monument to Engel goes up at Vicosoprano, in the Swiss valley of the Bregaglia. It is the only work of his life placed outside Italy, Romania, Egypt and the United States, and it widens the list of who writes to him. Latin kingdoms, emigrant colonies, now a valley of the Swiss republic: they want their civic dead cast by a man whose politics they know before they write. He is fifty-four, and his correspondence now runs through the lodges as much as through the ministries.
suggested_refs: The monument to Engel at Vicosoprano, Bregaglia, Switzerland, 1899
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Ferrari, Ettore'

stops.name: Milan, the monument to Carlo Cattaneo
stops.date_confidence: inaugurated 23 June 1901, the centenary of Cattaneo's birth, per it.wikipedia's article on the monument; Treccani dates the work 1893. Contradiction left open.
stops.campa: His Carlo Cattaneo is inaugurated in Via Santa Margherita on the hundredth birthday of the Milanese who wanted a federal Italy of free cities and got a centralised kingdom instead. Milan claims him back with a statue cut by a Roman republican. In this same year the Universita Popolare di Milano is founded, an evening school for working people, and Ferrari is named among its founders. The school and the statue are ordered by the same men in the same city in the same year.
suggested_refs: The Cattaneo monument, Via Santa Margherita, Milan; the Universita Popolare di Milano, 1901
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Ferrari, Ettore'

stops.name: Rome, the Aventine: the Mazzini commission
stops.date_confidence: commission attested to 1902 by it.wikipedia; month unrecorded, defaulted to January
stops.campa: The commission for a monument to Giuseppe Mazzini on the Aventine comes to him, and he begins the work that will outlive him. The sketch is ready by 1905, the siting approved in 1914, the first stone laid in 1922. Then Fascism, and the marble waits on the hill above the Circus Maximus while the prophet of the Roman Republic goes unhonoured by a regime that claims Rome for itself. He is fifty-seven, and he has taken on a stone that will need a second Italy before anyone can unveil it.
suggested_refs: The monument to Giuseppe Mazzini on the Aventine, commissioned 1902

stops.name: Rome, Palazzo Giustiniani: elected Grand Master
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The assembly of the Order elects him Grand Master of the Grande Oriente d'Italia, succeeding Ernesto Nathan, in the palace the Order has occupied since 1901. In his address he refuses the shadows: Freemasonry is to come down into contact with life and fight its battles in daylight. Under him the Order takes a frankly democratic and anticlerical line, for secular schools, civil marriage and divorce, and the politicisation costs it a schism in 1908. He will hold the office thirteen years.
stops.quote: la Massoneria non deve tenersi costantemente isolata e nell'ombra, ma scendere a contatto della vita, combattere alla luce del sole le sante battaglie dell'alta sua missione per la tutela della giustizia e per la grande educazione. Nuovi bisogni presentano nuovi problemi; nuovi problemi esigono nuove soluzioni; da nuovi doveri scaturiscono nuovi diritti. La Massoneria non può, non deve chiudere gli occhi alla nuova luce, ma fissarla, scrutarla e dirigerla.
stops.quote_source: Ettore Ferrari, inaugural address as Grand Master of the Grande Oriente d'Italia, 1904, quoted in it.wikipedia.org, 'Ettore Ferrari'
suggested_refs: Palazzo Giustiniani, seat of the Grande Oriente d'Italia from 21 April 1901
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Ferrari, Ettore'

stops.name: Rome, Palazzo Giustiniani: re-elected, and the presidency
stops.date_confidence: attested to the morning of 23 February 1906 by the Ars et Labor chronicle
stops.campa: The assembly returns him with a hundred and thirty-one votes of a hundred and forty-nine and elects Engel his assistant grand master. In the same year the Regio Istituto di belle arti makes him its president. He stands at the height of every office he will ever hold: head of Italian Freemasonry, head of a state school of art, city councillor, sculptor of the republic's dead. The newspapers count the Order's ballots the way they count a parliament's, and print the totals.
stops.quote: Stamane l'Assemblea Costituente della Massoneria ha rieletto a Gran Maestro Ettore Ferrari con voti 131 sopra 149 votanti, ed ha eletto a Gran Maestro Aggiunto l'on. Engel, con voti 110 su 132 votanti.
stops.quote_source: Ars et Labor, 1906, n. 3, chronicle column 'Il giro del mondo in un mese' (it.wikisource.org)
suggested_refs: Ars et Labor, 1906 n. 3, report of the Masonic assembly of 23 February 1906
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Ferrari, Ettore'

stops.name: Meldola, the medal for Felice Orsini
stops.date_confidence: attested to 9 May 1909 by it.wikipedia
stops.campa: At Meldola a medal struck with his portrait of Felice Orsini is presented, the town claiming its conspirator back in bronze. Ferrari's small work follows the same rule as his large: the men the state executed or drove out are given faces and set in public, at municipal expense, with the mayor standing by. He is sixty-four and Grand Master of the Order, and he is still modelling medals for provincial committees that cannot pay much and would not think of asking anyone else.
suggested_refs: The Felice Orsini medal presented at Meldola, 9 May 1909

stops.name: Trani, the monument to Giovanni Bovio
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Treccani's monument list; month unrecorded, defaulted to January
stops.campa: Trani receives his Giovanni Bovio, the positivist philosopher and republican deputy who sat with him on the far left, and Iseo receives his Gabriele Rosa the same year. The generation he served with in the Chamber is dying, and its survivors commission one another's monuments. He is sixty-nine and still the first name a republican committee writes down. In the summer Europe goes to war, and the Order he heads will spend three years arguing whether Italy should follow it in.
suggested_refs: The Giovanni Bovio monument at Trani and the Gabriele Rosa monument at Iseo, both 1914
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Ferrari, Ettore'

stops.name: Paris, the congress of the Entente lodges
stops.date_confidence: attested to June 1917 by Treccani; day unrecorded, defaulted to the first. Canonical Paris pin inherited from the corpus.
stops.campa: He goes to Paris for the congress of the masonic bodies of the Entente, called to draft a league of nations out of the war, and speaks there for the Italian Order. The Italian press turns on him for it: a Grand Master negotiating a peace order abroad, in wartime, at the head of a secret society. By the twenty-fifth of November the campaign has forced him to lay down the mandate he has held for thirteen years. He leaves the office at seventy-two with the Order whole and his name under attack.
suggested_refs: The 1917 Paris congress of Entente masonic obediences and its league of nations project
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Ferrari, Ettore'

stops.name: Rome, the Supreme Council and the refused senatorship
stops.date_confidence: the Scottish Rite appointment is dated 1918 and the honorary grand mastership and refusal 1919 by Treccani; months unrecorded, defaulted to January
stops.campa: Named honorary Grand Master for life, he is appointed Sovereign Grand Commander of the Supreme Council of the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite for Italy, the chair of the thirty-third degree, and he will hold it until he dies. The government offers him a senatorship for life. He refuses it on the ground of a lifetime's consistency: a republican does not enter the king's upper house by the king's appointment. He is seventy-four. He has taken the state's chair of sculpture and the state's commissions for twenty years and more, and will not take its title.
suggested_refs: The Supreme Council of the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite for Italy, 1918-1929
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Ferrari, Ettore'

stops.name: Rome, the death of Maria Carolina
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Maria Carolina Frey von Freienstein dies in Rome on the eighth of August, forty-two years married to him. In the same autumn the Fascists march on the city. He is seventy-seven, a widower, head of a Rite that the new government intends to abolish, and father of two sons, the younger named for the man in Campo de' Fiori and destined to fight the regime in the Resistance. The studio keeps working. The commissions still arrive, from Egypt, from America, from Romania.
suggested_refs: Giordano Bruno Ferrari, painter and anti-fascist, second son of the sculptor
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Ferrari, Ettore'

stops.name: Staten Island, the memorial to Antonio Meucci
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Treccani and by the museum's own record; month unrecorded, defaulted to January. No source places Ferrari in New York.
stops.campa: A memorial to Antonio Meucci is erected in the front yard of the cottage at Rosebank on Staten Island, the house where the inventor lived and where Garibaldi lodged with him during his American exile. Ferrari, who has spent thirty years setting Garibaldi in Italian squares, now supplies the American shrine of the house that sheltered him. The Italian emigration wants a pantheon of its own in New York harbour, and it sends to Rome, to the old Grand Master, for the bronze.
suggested_refs: The Meucci memorial at the Garibaldi-Meucci Museum, 420 Tompkins Avenue, Rosebank, Staten Island, erected 1923
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Ferrari, Ettore'

stops.name: Alexandria, the memorial to the Italian dead
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Treccani; month unrecorded, defaulted to January. The site within Alexandria is not specified in any source consulted.
stops.campa: For the Italian community of Alexandria he makes a memorial to their dead of the world war. The colony on the Egyptian shore, merchants and engineers and printers, buries its sons in Ferrari's stone. He is seventy-nine. The commissions of these last years come from the edges of the Italian world, Egypt, America, Romania, from communities that keep the lay and liberal Italy of the nineteenth century intact abroad while the peninsula itself is turning into something else.
suggested_refs: The war memorial for the Italian community of Alexandria, Egypt, 1924
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Ferrari, Ettore'

stops.name: Rome, Lux and the last open address
stops.date_confidence: Lux founded November 1923 per Treccani; the address is situated at the end of 1924 by the same entry, without a day, defaulted to 1 December
stops.campa: In November 1923 he founded Lux, a review in which the political and the esoteric business of the Order run down one column, and at the end of 1924 he calls on his brothers to hold the secular inheritance of the Risorgimento against a government that means to finish it. Freemasonry, he tells them, is not a party but a school, and almost a great lay church, gathering men of different political creeds around eternal human principles. It is his last public definition of the thing he leads.
stops.quote: La Massoneria non è un partito o una corrente politica, nel significato che comunemente si dà alla parola; ma una scuola e quasi vorremmo dire una grande chiesa laica che aduna e accorda uomini di diverso credo politico in un ordine più elevato di eterni principi umani.
stops.quote_source: Ettore Ferrari, quoted without footnote in the Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani (Treccani), 'Ferrari, Ettore', situated at the end of 1924
suggested_refs: Lux, the masonic review founded by Ferrari in November 1923
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Ferrari, Ettore'

stops.name: Sulmona, the Ovid returned to his birthplace
stops.date_confidence: year attested by it.wikipedia and en.wikipedia; month unrecorded, defaulted to January
stops.campa: A replica of the Constanta Ovid is installed at Sulmona, the poet's birthplace in Abruzzo, thirty-eight years after the original went up on the Black Sea. The exile comes home in a second cast, nineteen centuries after Augustus sent him out. The same figure now stands in two countries, on the shore of his banishment and in the town that bore him. Ferrari is eighty when it is set in place, four years from being watched by policemen for belonging to an order the government has outlawed.
suggested_refs: The replica Ovid at Sulmona, Abruzzo, 1925

stops.name: Rome, the law against secret societies
stops.date_confidence: law n. 2029 of 26 November 1925, passed by the Chamber 19 May 1925; the November 1926 measures often cited instead dissolved non-Fascist associations generally
stops.campa: Law number two thousand and twenty-nine requires associations to declare their members, and it is aimed at Freemasonry and nothing else. The Grande Oriente d'Italia suspends its works that same month; lodges are sacked, papers seized, and Ferrari, at the head of the Scottish Rite, dissolves nothing. Mussolini's government does not need to abolish the Order by name in order to end it. He is eighty, under surveillance, and continues to act as the head of a body that is no longer permitted to meet.
suggested_refs: Law n. 2029 of 26 November 1925 on secret societies; the suspension of the works of the Grande Oriente d'Italia
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Ferrari, Ettore'

stops.name: Cluj, Trajan and Decebalus
stops.date_confidence: year attested by en.wikipedia and it.wikipedia; month unrecorded, defaulted to January. Coordinate is a city pin, the works' sites are not specified.
stops.campa: Romania sends for him a third time. For Cluj he makes a bust of the emperor Trajan, a bust of the Dacian king Decebalus, and a relief of Trajan with the Capitoline Wolf: conqueror and conquered given the same treatment, the Latin descent of Transylvania argued in bronze by an eighty-two-year-old Roman. It is his last large commission, and he works it out in a city where the order he still heads has been driven underground and the ministries no longer answer his letters.
suggested_refs: The Trajan and Decebalus busts and the Capitoline Wolf relief at Cluj-Napoca, 1927

stops.name: Rome, Campo de' Fiori: the statue the concordat cannot move
stops.date_confidence: the Lateran Pacts are signed 11 February 1929; it.wikipedia dates the Church's request for the statue's removal to the negotiations, without a day
stops.campa: Negotiating the Lateran Pacts, the Church asks for the removal of the bronze in Campo de' Fiori and offers an expiatory chapel in its place. Mussolini refuses: the statue will remain where it is. In the same breath he forbids the commemorations at its feet. Ferrari, six months from death and watched by the police, keeps the one work of his that a concordat cannot undo, because forty years after the unveiling a dictatorship finds his heretic useful against a pope.
suggested_refs: The Lateran Pacts of 11 February 1929 and the Church's request for the removal of the Bruno monument

stops.name: Rome, the powers passed to Giuseppe Leti
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Denounced for attempting to reorganise Freemasonry under the ban, he is given a formal police warning, and he transmits his whole masonic authority to Giuseppe Leti in France, so that the succession continues beyond the reach of the Italian state. He is eighty-four. The order he brought out into daylight in 1904 goes back into shadow and exile, carried out of the country in a letter, three months before the hand that signed the letter stops working.
suggested_refs: The transfer of Ferrari's masonic powers to Giuseppe Leti, 25 May 1929
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Ferrari, Ettore'

stops.name: Rome, the Verano
stops.date_confidence: death attested to 19 August 1929, aged 84; the en.wikipedia infobox gives 86 and a stray 1931, one arithmetic error with two faces. Burial in the Verano attested by his own article rather than by the cemetery's.
stops.campa: He dies in Rome on the nineteenth of August, eighty-four years old, and is buried in the Cimitero del Verano among the funerary monuments he had carved for other men's graves. Of the offices he held, none outlive him: the Order suspended, the Rite in exile, the left of the Chamber dispersed, the council seat long behind him. Of the statues, all outlive him. The Mazzini on the Aventine is not yet cut, and his son Giordano Bruno Ferrari will live to see it standing.
suggested_refs: The Cimitero del Verano, Piazzale del Verano 1, Rome
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Ferrari, Ettore'

stops.name: Rome, Campo de' Fiori: the seventeenth of February
stops.date_confidence: the sources record only that the gatherings resumed after the fall of Fascism and recur every 17 February; the year 1945 is a placement, not an attested date
stops.campa: With Fascism fallen, the freethinkers come back to Campo de' Fiori on the seventeenth of February, the day of the burning, and the gathering becomes annual again: Masons, atheists, pantheists, students, and a representative of the city government of Rome laying a wreath at the foot of the plinth while the flower market packs up around them. Ferrari's bronze has stopped being a thing people look at and become a place people stand, once a year, in the same square.
suggested_refs: The annual 17 February commemoration at the Bruno monument, Campo de' Fiori

stops.name: Rome, the Aventine: Mazzini unveiled at last
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the second of June, the third anniversary of the republic, the monument to Giuseppe Mazzini is inaugurated on the Aventine, forty-seven years after the commission and twenty years after the death of the sculptor; his son Giordano Bruno Ferrari, painter and Resistance man, saw the work resumed the year before. Mazzini looks out over the Circus Maximus in a republic at last. The stone waited out the monarchy that approved its siting and the regime that halted the work, and went up on a republican holiday.
suggested_refs: The Mazzini monument on the Aventine, inaugurated 2 June 1949

stops.name: Rome, Campo de' Fiori: Luther found in the medallion
stops.date_confidence: year attested by it.wikipedia and en.wikipedia; month and day of the identification unrecorded, defaulted to January
stops.campa: The Swedish historian Lars Berggren, reading the pedestal medallion by medallion, finds inside the relief of Lucilio Vanini a small concealed portrait of Martin Luther, worked into the bronze in 1889 and unnoticed for a hundred and two years. Ferrari had set the arch-heretic of the north on a monument at the papacy's door and told nobody. The statue that Leo XIII condemned by name had been carrying, the whole time, one more accusation that no one had yet read.
suggested_refs: Lars Berggren's 1991 identification of the concealed Luther portrait in the Vanini medallion
